title: Sins first (Mark 2:1–12)
hookLine: the paralyzed man hears his sins forgiven before he hears walk
tomorrow: the sabbath was made for man

lines: A HOLE, AND A MAT ON ROPES.
cards: Jesus is back in Capernaum, word gets around, and the house is so packed there's no room even at the door. Four men arrive carrying their friend on a mat. He can't walk.

So they do what good friends do when the front door fails: they climb onto the flat roof, dig a hole straight through it, and lower him down on ropes, right in front of Jesus, while dust and bits of roof fall on everybody's heads.
Everyone knows what the man needs. And Jesus says something nobody expects.

teach.h: THEY CARRIED HIM ON THEIR FAITH.
teach.b: First, whose faith. Mark says Jesus saw their faith, the friends' faith. The man on the mat hasn't said a word; somebody else's trust carried him in.
Second, the surprise. Jesus looks at him and says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Son, thy sins are forgiven thee." Not get up.
Not be healed. Forgiven. The friends must have looked at each other: that's not what we came for.

Third, the scribes. Some teachers of the law sit there, thinking it silently: "Why doth this man speak thus? he blasphemeth. Who can forgive sins, but God only?" In one way, they've understood exactly.
Only God can forgive sins against God, and that's the point Mark wants you to feel.
Then Jesus asks: which is easier, to say your sins are forgiven, or to say get up and walk? Anyone can say the first; nobody can check it.

teach.h: WHO CAN FORGIVE SINS BUT GOD?
teach.b: So, to show that the Son of man has power on earth to forgive sins, he tells the man: arise, take up thy bed, and go home. And he does, in front of everyone. Fourth, what it doesn't mean.
Jesus never says the man's sin caused his paralysis; the gospels push back against that idea elsewhere.
The story is about order: the deeper healing first, the one nobody could see.

teach.h: SON, THY SINS ARE FORGIVEN THEE.
teach.b: Catholics hear in this story the root of confession. They believe Christ gave his apostles a share in this power to forgive, and that it continues in the sacrament of reconciliation today.

how: Catholics receive forgiveness in the sacrament of reconciliation, or confession, where a priest speaks the words of absolution; this gospel is read at Sunday Mass in Ordinary Time.

o: the man must confess before he can be healed
Jesus forgives the man before he heals his legs
Jesus says the man's sins caused his paralysis

games.q: who did what — tap the pairs.
p: who can forgive sins but God?

s: Mark says Jesus saw the paralyzed man's faith
he saw their faith: the friends who carried him.
Jesus said the man's sin caused his paralysis
he never says that. the story is about healing the deeper wound first.
the scribes were right that only God forgives sins
that's the point Mark wants you to feel about who Jesus is.

games.q: a paralyzed man has just been lowered through the roof in front of you. everyone expects you to heal his legs. what does Jesus say first?
o: son, thy sins are forgiven thee.
games.why: "Son, thy sins are forgiven thee." the healing of his legs comes second, as a sign of the first.

practice: Start with what you think you need today, a fix, an answer, more time, and name it. Then go one layer down: maybe it's to be forgiven, or to forgive, or rest, or to stop being afraid.
If you pray, ask God for that deeper thing; if you don't, just name it honestly to yourself.

wordCard.voice: Sins first. The paralyzed man hears forgiven before he hears walk: Jesus heals the deeper wound before the visible one. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: are forgiven, from aphiēmi, to let go, release.

carryVoice: Your line: the deeper healing first. The walking came second. That's day one hundred ninety-seven.
